passage: The power went off just as the biscuit tin came out, and only three biscuits were left inside. Yamini, five, held the tin in the candlelight. She pushed one straight into her brother Vaibhav's hand without a word. Then Mummy's friend's daughter, a girl Yamini had met only that evening, held out her palm. Yamini pulled the tin to her chest. She looked at Mummy. She looked at the girl. Slowly she broke the last biscuit and gave the smaller half, her eyes on Vaibhav, who was already crunching happily.

qa.q: How many biscuits were left in the tin?
qa.a: Only three biscuits were left inside.

qa.q: What does Yamini pulling the tin to her chest suggest she felt when the visiting girl held out her palm?
qa.a: She seems unsure and protective, not ready to share easily with a girl she had met only that evening.

qa.q: How could Mummy gently help Yamini at that moment?
qa.a: Mummy could sit close, say the guest's name, and smile at the half biscuit, so the new girl feels less like a stranger.

qa.q: What might it be like for the visiting girl to get a small half while Vaibhav gets a whole biscuit?
qa.a: She might feel a bit left out, yet pleased to get anything at all in a new house on a dark evening.

grounding: A young child gives her brother a treat at once but shares only slowly and a little with a visitor's child she has just met.

passage: In the fourth-floor flat, Eshaan, five, sat on the floor with a bowl of mango slices. "Dadi, open!" he said, and popped the biggest piece into her mouth, giggling when juice ran down her chin. Then the doorbell rang. A new neighbour came in with a boy called Mridul, who sat down quietly and looked at the bowl. Eshaan turned his back a little and ate two slices fast. Dadi said nothing, only waited. After a while Eshaan held out one small slice, his arm stretched as far as it would go, and pulled it back the moment Mridul took it.

qa.q: Who did Eshaan feed the biggest mango piece to?
qa.a: Eshaan popped the biggest piece into Dadi's mouth.

qa.q: Why might Eshaan have turned his back and eaten two slices fast when Mridul arrived?
qa.a: He probably felt wary of the new boy and wanted to keep the mango for himself and Dadi, the person he feels close to.

qa.q: Dadi chose to wait instead of telling Eshaan to share. Why might that work?
qa.a: Waiting let Eshaan decide by himself, so the small slice he offered came from him rather than from an order 🙂

qa.q: What might the afternoon be like for Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul may feel shy and outside the family's warmth, and the stretched-out arm shows he is still a stranger to Eshaan.

grounding: A young child happily feeds his grandmother but is slow and hesitant to share with a visiting neighbour's child.

passage:
"Chinmay, Mridul bhaiya is home!" called Mamma.
Chinmay ran with his packet of chips. "Bhaiya, take, take! You get the big ones."
"Thanks, champ." Mridul crunched loudly.
The doorbell rang. Papa's office friend came in with a small girl in a yellow frock.
"Chinmay, this is Tia. Will you share with her?" Mamma asked.
Chinmay hugged the packet. "It's for bhaiya."
"Bhaiya already has some."
"She doesn't know me."
Mridul crouched down. "Give her one, and I'll give you my big one back."
Chinmay looked at Tia for a long time. Then he held out a single broken chip.

qa.q: What did Chinmay tell Mridul he could take?
qa.a: Chinmay said, "Bhaiya, take, take! You get the big ones."

qa.q: What does Chinmay's line "She doesn't know me" show about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels shy and unsure about sharing with Tia because she is a stranger, while bhaiya feels like his own.

qa.q: Was Mridul's offer a good way to nudge Chinmay, and what else might help?
qa.a: It helped him take a first small step; letting Chinmay and Tia play together for a while might make sharing easier next time.

qa.q: How might Tia feel getting one broken chip after watching bhaiya get the big ones?
qa.a: Tia might feel shy or a little left out, though glad to be offered something in a house full of strangers.

grounding: A young child shares eagerly with his older brother but only reluctantly with a visitor's child who is a stranger to him.

passage:
Playschool note, Grandparents' Day. Written by Zainab Ma'am.

Vikas, four, was thrilled when his Nana arrived. He pushed the bigger half of his laddoo into Nana's mouth, laughing. Then Pooja's cousin, visiting for the day, came and stood next to him, looking at the box. Vikas pulled the box close and turned his back. When I asked if she could have one, he whispered, "She's not my family." At last, with Nana nodding, he held out the smallest piece.

What I did next: I sat them together for the clay game, so they would not be strangers.

qa.q: Who did Vikas give the bigger half of his laddoo to?
qa.a: He gave it to his Nana.

qa.q: Why did Vikas whisper 'She's not my family'?
qa.a: He felt close and generous with his Nana but unsure and less willing to share with a child he did not know.

qa.q: How did the teacher help, and why might it work?
qa.a: She sat the two children together for the clay game so they could get to know each other, which could make sharing feel easier next time.

qa.q: How might Pooja's cousin feel when Vikas turns his back?
qa.a: The visiting child might feel left out and shy, standing near a box of sweets in a place where she knows almost no one.

grounding: A four-year-old shares eagerly with his grandfather but is slow to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Lakshmi, five, sat with a ripe guava. She bit it, then held it up. "Ammamma, you have!" Ammamma took a tiny bite and laughed. Lakshmi gave a big piece to her little brother too. Then the milkman came with his small son, who stood by the gate staring. Lakshmi hid the guava behind her back. Her big sister Alka said, "Share one piece?" Lakshmi shook her head. "He's not ours." Alka waited. The boy kept looking. At last Lakshmi walked over and held out a small piece, then ran back to Ammamma's lap.

qa.q: Who did Lakshmi give the first bite of her guava to?
qa.a: She gave it to Ammamma.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi hiding the guava suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels generous with her own family but shy and protective with a boy she does not know.

qa.q: What did Alka do that helped Lakshmi share?
qa.a: Alka asked gently and then waited, giving Lakshmi time to decide for herself instead of forcing her.

qa.q: What is it like for the milkman's son standing at the gate?
qa.a: He is a visitor watching other children share a treat, which might make him feel shy and left out.

grounding: A five-year-old happily shares with her grandmother and brother but is slow to share with the milkman's son.

passage:
Preschool note, Tuesday.
Harish (5) brought a packet of biscuits today. At snack time, his younger brother Asif came over from the toddler room, and Harish immediately gave him two, then broke another in half so they'd have the same. Later, a new boy visiting with his mother sat at the table and looked at the packet. Harish held it close and ate slowly, not offering. When I asked him to share, he gave one, a little reluctantly. I'll try pairing Harish with the visiting child in a game tomorrow so they get to know each other before snack time.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Harish give Asif first?
qa.a: Harish immediately gave him two.

qa.q: What does Harish holding the packet close suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Harish felt protective of his biscuits and wary of the new boy, whom he didn't know yet.

qa.q: Why is pairing Harish with the visiting child in a game a good idea?
qa.a: Getting to know the boy may make him feel less like a stranger, so Harish may share more easily.

qa.q: How might the visiting boy have felt watching Harish?
qa.a: The visiting boy may have felt left out and shy, wanting a biscuit but new to the group.

grounding: A young child shares biscuits readily with his brother but is slower to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage: In the courtyard of their house near Thrissur, Joseph, five, sat with a ripe mango. When his big brother Siddharth came home from school, Joseph ran to him and held out a juicy piece. "For you, chetta!" Then he took a slice to Appachan, his grandfather, on the veranda. But when the neighbour's visiting nephew, a boy Joseph didn't know, peeped over the wall, Joseph turned his back and ate quickly. Appachan called, "Share one with the guest, mone." Joseph handed over the smallest slice, frowning, then ran back to sit close to Siddharth.

qa.q: What did Joseph call Siddharth when he gave him mango?
qa.a: He said, "For you, chetta!"

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when the visiting boy peeped over the wall?
qa.a: Joseph felt wary and possessive, not yet trusting the boy he didn't know.

qa.q: How could Appachan help Joseph share more freely?
qa.a: Appachan could invite the visiting boy to sit with them, so Joseph gets to know him and sees him as less of a stranger.

qa.q: How might the visiting nephew have felt getting the smallest slice?
qa.a: The nephew may have felt a little unwelcome and awkward, being new and given the smallest piece.

grounding: A young child readily shares mango with his brother and grandfather but is slower to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage: In their Amman flat, Rania, five, was eating date cookies on the rug. Her baby brother Alejandro crawled over, and she put a cookie right into his hand. Then she carried one to Teta in the kitchen. Later, Mama's friend came with her little girl, whom Rania had never seen. The girl sat on the rug and looked at the plate. Rania pulled it closer and turned away. "Rania, share," Mama said softly. Rania held out one cookie, arm straight, not looking at the girl. Then she scooted over to sit by Alejandro.

qa.q: What did Rania put into Alejandro's hand?
qa.a: She put a cookie right into his hand.

qa.q: How can you tell Rania felt unsure about the visiting girl?
qa.a: She pulled the plate closer, turned away and held out a cookie without looking, showing she felt wary of a stranger.

qa.q: What might help Rania feel more generous toward the visitor?
qa.a: A short game together first could help Rania see the girl as a friend, not a stranger.

qa.q: How might the visiting girl have felt?
qa.a: The visiting girl may have felt shy and left out in a new home, being handed a cookie so stiffly.

grounding: A young child shares readily with her brother and grandmother but is slower to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage:
It was the Christmas party at the playschool, and snow-white cotton was stuck on every window. Each child got one slice of plum cake.
Chetan broke his slice in half at once and ran to his little sister Rukmini in the next room. "Rukku! For you!"
Back at his table, the new girl who had come that week looked at his crumbs. She had dropped her slice on the floor.
Chetan pulled his plate closer. He looked at her, then at the plate. After a long time he gave her the smallest corner.
"Thank you," she whispered.

qa.q: What did each child get at the party?
qa.a: Each child got one slice of plum cake.

qa.q: Why did Chetan run to Rukmini so quickly with half his cake?
qa.a: He felt close to his little sister and happy to share with her, without even stopping to think.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Chetan share with the new girl?
qa.a: The teacher could introduce her by name and have them play together, so she feels less like a stranger to him.

qa.q: What might the new girl be feeling when she looks at Chetan's crumbs?
qa.a: She is probably sad and hopeful, having dropped her own slice and not knowing anyone yet.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing a treat readily with his sister but slowly with a new child at a festive party.

passage:
Monday, the first rainy day: Mummy cut a mango. Vishal ran with the biggest piece to Dadi, who was sitting by the window. "Dadi, you eat!" Then he gave one to his sister Pooja.
Wednesday, still raining: A neighbour aunty came with her son. Mummy put out a bowl of mango. Vishal sat on the bowl's edge with his arms around it. "Mine," he said. The boy looked at his mother.
Saturday: The boy came again. This time he brought paper boats for the puddles. They played all afternoon. At snack time, Vishal pushed the mango bowl toward him. "You have some."

qa.q: Who did Vishal give the biggest piece of mango to?
qa.a: He gave the biggest piece to Dadi.

qa.q: Why did Vishal put his arms around the mango bowl on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt unsure and protective with a boy he didn't know, so he wasn't ready to share with him.

qa.q: What helped Vishal share with the neighbour's boy by Saturday?
qa.a: Playing with paper boats all afternoon made the boy feel like a friend, so Vishal felt close enough to share.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's boy have felt on Wednesday?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and shy, looking at his mother when Vishal said "Mine."

grounding: Shows a young child sharing easily with grandmother and sister but slow to share with a visiting child until they become closer.

passage:
On Pongal morning the village street smelled of sweet pongal and wet kolam powder. Lakshmi had one last piece of sugarcane, and her cousin Madhuri had none.
"Here, akka," Lakshmi said, and broke it with her teeth, giving Madhuri the bigger half.
Then a girl from the bus that had broken down at the corner came near. She was from another village, waiting for her father. She stared at the sugarcane.
Lakshmi turned her back and chewed. Madhuri nudged her. Lakshmi looked at the girl, then at her small half. Slowly she held out a tiny bit.
The girl smiled. Lakshmi smiled too, just a little.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi have one last piece of?
qa.a: Lakshmi had one last piece of sugarcane.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi turn her back when the girl from the bus came near?
qa.a: She felt shy and unwilling to share with a stranger, though she had shared easily with her cousin.

qa.q: What small step helped Lakshmi share with the stranger?
qa.a: Madhuri's gentle nudge helped Lakshmi notice the girl and offer a small bit.

qa.q: What is it like for the girl from the bus, waiting on a festival morning?
qa.a: She probably feels lonely and a bit left out, far from her own village and watching others eat.

grounding: Shows a young child giving her cousin the bigger half of a treat but slow to share with a stranger's child on a festival morning.

passage: Diwali evening, and the flat glowed with diyas. "One for Samir!" Vaibhav pushed a laddoo into his little brother's fist. "One for Dadi!" Dadi pretended to faint with joy. Then the new neighbours came in with a girl in a sparkly frock. She looked at the box. Vaibhav slid it behind his back. Mummy crouched. "She's our guest." He looked at the girl's shoes, then at Samir chewing happily. Slowly he held up the smallest laddoo. The girl took it and smiled. Vaibhav smiled back, just a little.

qa.q: What was the first thing Vaibhav gave Samir?
qa.a: He pushed a laddoo into his little brother's fist.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav slide the box behind his back?
qa.a: He felt shy and unsure about the new girl; sharing with his brother and Dadi felt easy, but a stranger's child felt different and he was reluctant.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Vaibhav share with new people next time?

qa.q: What might the girl in the sparkly frock feel when the box disappears?

grounding: Shows a young child sharing readily with his brother and grandmother but more slowly with a visiting child.

passage: It was the hottest week of May. "Hemant Nanu, one for you!" Ishita held out a whole slice of mango. "Only if you eat one too," Nanu laughed. A boy from the next bench in the park stood watching, thumb in his mouth. "Ishita, he's looking at the mangoes." "He's not our family." "Does that mean he can't have any?" Ishita hugged the box. "I don't know him." "You could ask his name." "What's your name?" she called. The boy mumbled. She put one small piece on a leaf and held it out at arm's length.

qa.q: What did Ishita hold out to Hemant Nanu?
qa.a: She held out a whole slice of mango.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she hugged the mango box?
qa.a: She felt wary and protective; the boy was a stranger, and sharing with someone who wasn't family made her hesitant.

qa.q: What small step did Nanu suggest to help Ishita share?
qa.a: He suggested she ask the boy's name, which makes a stranger feel less strange.

qa.q: How might the boy from the next bench see Ishita's piece on a leaf?
qa.a: He might feel pleased but still shy, noticing it came at arm's length and that she shared much more easily with Nanu.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who shares freely with her grandfather but hesitates with an unknown child.

passage: Nursery note, January winter picnic. Jatin's cousin Mohit visited today. At snack time Jatin pushed half his orange across the mat to Mohit: "This is my brother-cousin." Later a girl who joined this week sat near Jatin. He turned his back and ate his segments quickly. I didn't force sharing. I sat with both and said, "This is Tia. She likes oranges too." Jatin stared, then offered one segment, fast, and looked at me. Next steps: pair Jatin with Tia for garden jobs so they get to know each other.

qa.q: What did Jatin call Mohit?
qa.a: "My brother-cousin."

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling when he turned his back on the new child?
qa.a: He probably felt shy and wary, because the new child was unfamiliar to him while Mohit was family.

qa.q: Why might pairing Jatin with Tia for garden jobs help?
qa.a: Spending time together can make Tia feel familiar to Jatin, and children share more easily with people they feel close to.

qa.q: What is it like for Tia when Jatin turns his back?
qa.a: Tia may feel left out and uncertain in her first week, watching someone share with one child and not with her.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing easily with a cousin and more slowly with an unfamiliar child.

passage: It is mango season in the village, and Nikita, five, has three pieces of peanut chikki from the weekly market. She runs to the courtyard and pops one into Ajji's mouth. "For you!" She gives one to her baby brother, who drools on it happily. Then Harish arrives with his mother, a visitor from the next village. He stares at the last piece. Nikita hides it behind her back and looks at her toes. "Share, Nikita," Ajji says softly. Nikita chews her lip for a long time. Then she breaks off a tiny corner and holds it out.

qa.q: How many pieces of peanut chikki did Nikita have?
qa.a: Three pieces.

qa.q: Why does Nikita hide the last piece behind her back?
qa.a: She feels shy and unsure with Harish, a visitor she doesn't know, so sharing feels much harder than with Ajji or her brother.

qa.q: How could Ajji help Nikita share with visitors?
qa.a: Ajji can gently encourage her, praise the tiny corner she gives, and help the two children play so Harish feels less like a stranger.

qa.q: What is it like for Harish when Nikita hides the chikki?

grounding: A young child shares treats easily with her grandmother and brother but is slow to share with a visiting child.
